name: Port scan
description: Scan the company's public servers to find open ports and the software versions behind them.

name: Phishing email
description: Send a fake email that tricks an employee into opening a malicious attachment or typing their password on a fake login page.

name: Exploit the web shop
description: Use a known vulnerability in outdated software on an internet-facing server, such as an old CMS or PHP version.

name: Password brute force
description: Try thousands of common passwords against a login page until one works.

name: Privilege escalation
description: Exploit a bug in the operating system or a service to turn a normal account into an administrator.

name: Move through Remote Desktop
description: Use stolen credentials to log in to other machines on the network through Remote Desktop.

name: Steal the data
description: Copy valuable data out of the company over the attacker's own connection.

name: Ransomware
description: Encrypt the company's files and demand money to unlock them.

name: Credential Stuffing
description: Try usernames and passwords leaked from other websites, hoping an employee reused the same password at work.

name: Exploit the VPN gateway
description: Use a known flaw in an unpatched VPN appliance to get onto the company network without any password.

name: Malicious Office macro
description: Email a Word or Excel file that runs hidden code when the employee clicks 'Enable content'.

name: Infected USB stick
description: Leave a USB stick labelled 'Salaries 2026' near the office and wait for someone to plug it in.

name: Bribe an insider
description: Pay an employee to hand over their login. Quiet and hard to spot, but expensive and not everyone says yes.

name: Wipe the data
description: Delete everything on a machine so the company cannot work. No ransom, just damage.

name: Password spraying
description: Try one common password, like 'Winter2026!', against many accounts, slowly enough to avoid lockouts.

name: MFA fatigue
description: Flood an employee's phone with login approval requests until they tap 'Approve' just to make it stop.

name: Cloud account takeover
description: Log in to the bank's cloud office suite with a password leaked or bought online.

name: Breach the IT vendor
description: Hack the outside company that does remote IT support for the bank, then use its trusted access.

name: Kerberoasting
description: Ask Active Directory for service tickets, take them home and crack the service account passwords offline.

name: Pass-the-Hash
description: Dump password hashes from a machine where you are admin, then log in elsewhere with the hash, no password needed.

name: DCSync
description: Pretend to be a domain controller and ask the real one to send you every password in the company.

name: Business email compromise
description: Email the finance team pretending to be the CEO or a supplier and ask for an urgent payment to a new account.

name: Steal a session cookie
description: Malware that steals browser data copies an employee's logged-in session, so the attacker gets in without the password or the MFA prompt.

name: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing
description: A fake login page sits between the employee and the real one and keeps the session after they pass MFA, so even a phone prompt does not save them.

name: Call the help desk
description: Phone the IT help desk pretending to be an employee who lost their phone, and ask them to reset the password and MFA.

name: Malicious app consent
description: Trick an employee into approving a harmless-looking app that asks to read their mail and files. No password needed, and it survives a password change.

name: Remote support tool
description: Install a legitimate remote support tool with a stolen account and use it to reach another machine. It looks like normal IT work.

name: Dump passwords from memory
description: With admin rights on a machine, copy the memory of the Windows login process and pull out the passwords of everyone who logs in there.

name: Golden Ticket
description: With admin rights on the domain controller, forge a Kerberos ticket that the whole domain trusts, and become anyone you like.

name: Upload to cloud storage
description: Copy the data to a public cloud storage service. The traffic looks like an employee saving a file.

name: DNS tunneling
description: Hide the data inside a stream of DNS lookups, which almost no firewall blocks. Slow and very quiet.

name: Delete the backups
description: With admin rights on a machine, delete its backups and shadow copies first, so ransomware there cannot be undone. Immutable backups resist it.
